h1: The 6 Best NAS Hard Drives and Storage Picks for Home Office of 2026, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best NAS Drives Home Office 2026: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: one CMR NAS drive and five enclosures and ready-to-use NAS units for home office storage, with the tradeoffs that matter.
mainKeyword: nas hard drives for home office
summary: The WD Red Plus 8TB is the one true NAS drive here and our top pick, because its CMR recording is the safest choice for RAID rebuilds. The Synology DS225+ is the best 2-bay enclosure to put it in, and the DS925+ suits growing storage. The Buffalo LinkStation is the only unit that arrives with a drive installed.
intro: The most common NAS mistake is buying a cheap desktop drive for a RAID box. Drives that use shingled recording can stall for hours during a rebuild, and that is exactly when you need them to behave. A NAS drive worth buying lists CMR recording and is built to spin around the clock.

Only one product in this list is a bare drive, so we paired it with the enclosures and ready-made units you would actually put it in. We reviewed them on paper, ranked on specs and owner feedback, and show price as a bucket.

products.name: Western Digital 8TB WD Red Plus NAS Internal Hard Drive
products.verdict: The safe CMR drive to fill an empty bay.
products.description:
The WD Red Plus is an 8TB 3.5 inch SATA drive with CMR recording, 256MB cache and 5640 RPM. It lands in the $200-500 bucket and ships as a bare drive with no enclosure.

It ranks first because it is the only actual hard drive here, and CMR is what makes it safe for RAID rebuilds. The enclosures below are good, but none of them stores a byte until you add drives like this one.

Buy it if you already own a NAS and need to fill a bay. The caveat is that the 5640 RPM design favors quiet and cool running over peak speed.
products.idealFor: Owners with an empty NAS bay who need a reliable drive.
products.skipIf: You have no NAS enclosure yet.

products.name: Synology DS225+ 2-Bay Diskless NAS with Hardware Transcoding
products.verdict: Polished DSM software on a compact 2-bay box.
products.description:
The Synology DS225+ is a 2-bay diskless NAS with an Intel CPU, hardware transcoding and the DSM software platform. It supports RAID 1 mirroring and sits in the $200-500 bucket.

It ranks above the UGREEN options because DSM is the more mature software, and it beats the DS925+ for most home offices because two mirrored drives are enough. The tradeoff is that two bays cap your expansion.

It suits a home office wanting mirrored backup plus some media duty. The caveat is that no drives are included, so budget for two.
products.idealFor: Small offices wanting mirrored drives and easy software.
products.skipIf: You expect to need more than two drives.

products.name: Synology DS925+ 4-Bay DiskStation (Diskless)
products.verdict: Four bays and RAID 5 for a growing office.
products.description:
The Synology DS925+ is a 4-bay diskless unit running DSM, with RAID 5 and RAID 10 support. It falls in the $500+ bucket and is designed for expanding storage.

It ranks third because it costs more than the DS225+ and most home offices will not fill four bays. Against the UGREEN DXP4800 Plus, it trades raw CPU headroom for Synology's software.

Choose it if you expect storage needs to grow. The caveat is that four drives plus the unit is the largest outlay in this guide.
products.idealFor: Offices expecting storage to expand over time.
products.skipIf: Two mirrored drives will be enough.

products.name: UGREEN NAS DXP4800 Plus 4-Bay with Intel Pentium Gold CPU
products.verdict: A 4-bay box with CPU headroom for several services.
products.description:
The UGREEN DXP4800 Plus is a 4-bay diskless NAS with an Intel Pentium Gold 8505 5-core CPU and RAID 5 or RAID 10 support. It sits in the $500+ bucket.

It ranks fourth because the Synology DS925+ offers a more established software ecosystem, while this model gives you more compute for transcoding and running multiple services.

It suits buyers who plan to run several apps alongside storage. The caveat is that no drives are included.
products.idealFor: Power users running transcoding and multiple services.
products.skipIf: You only need simple file storage.

products.name: BUFFALO LinkStation 210 4TB 1-Bay NAS (Hard Drive Included)
products.verdict: The simplest start, with a 4TB drive already installed.
products.description:
The Buffalo LinkStation 210 is a 1-bay NAS that ships with a 4TB drive installed. It falls in the $100-200 bucket and works as home cloud or network storage straight away.

It ranks fifth because a single bay means no RAID redundancy, so a drive failure risks your data. Against the diskless units, it is the only one that needs no extra purchase.

It suits someone who wants shared storage with minimal setup. The caveat is that you should back up important files elsewhere.
products.skipIf: You need redundancy or room to grow.

products.name: UGREEN NAS DH2300 2-Bay Desktop NAS (Diskless)
products.verdict: Basic 2-bay redundancy at the lowest enclosure price.
products.description:
The UGREEN DH2300 is a compact 2-bay diskless desktop NAS that supports up to 64TB total with drives sold separately. It falls in the $100-200 bucket.

It ranks last because the Synology DS225+ offers more software polish and processing power. What you get here is basic 2-bay RAID at an entry price.

It suits budget buyers who want simple mirrored storage. The caveat is limited compute, so skip it for heavy transcoding.
products.skipIf: You want transcoding or advanced apps.

methodology.title: Recording type
methodology.description: CMR drives were treated as the safe default for RAID, and drives or units without that detail got less credit.

methodology.title: Bay count and RAID
methodology.description: More bays and RAID 5 or 10 support scored higher for redundancy and growth.

methodology.title: Software platform
methodology.description: We weighed Synology DSM against other platforms for maturity and ease of use.

methodology.title: Compute headroom
methodology.description: CPU and hardware transcoding mattered for media and multi-service workloads.

methodology.title: Total cost to run
methodology.description: Because most units ship without drives, we counted the added drive spend.

whatMatters.detail: CMR writes tracks separately, while SMR overlaps them to pack in more data. SMR can slow badly during a RAID rebuild, which is when your data is most at risk. Look for CMR in the specs or the maker's drive list before buying.
One bay has no redundancy, two bays allow mirroring, and four bays allow RAID 5 or RAID 10. More bays cost more upfront but make growth easier. Count the drives you will need in three years.
Most enclosures here are diskless, so the real cost is the unit plus drives. A bundled unit like the Buffalo is cheaper to start. Read the listing for the phrase diskless or hard drive included.
A stronger CPU handles media conversion and several apps at once. For plain file sharing a basic chip is enough. Check whether hardware transcoding is listed if you stream video.
The software controls backups, sharing and apps. Synology's DSM is widely used and polished. Look at what the listing says about the platform before you commit.

howToChoose.intro: A NAS needs both an enclosure and drives, so start with what you already own.

cards.label: Diskless
cards.text: Diskless units like the Synology and UGREEN models cost more overall but give redundancy and growth with drives such as the WD Red Plus.

howToChoose.note: Most home offices should default to a diskless 2-bay and add CMR drives.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Simple setup, clear software and a CMR drive so a rebuild will not stall.

cards.text: Pair the Synology DS225+ with the WD Red Plus, or start with the Buffalo LinkStation for zero setup.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You need RAID 5 or 10 and room to grow, which means the Synology DS925+ or UGREEN DXP4800 Plus.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You only need basic backup, where the UGREEN DH2300 or Buffalo LinkStation 210 is enough.

faq.q: Can I use a regular desktop drive in a NAS?
faq.a: You can, but it may not be built for constant operation. A NAS-rated CMR drive like the WD Red Plus is the safer choice.

faq.q: What is the biggest NAS mistake?
faq.a: Buying an SMR drive, which can stall during RAID rebuilds. Check for CMR first.

faq.q: Is the DS925+ worth it over the DS225+?
faq.a: Only if you will use more than two drives. Otherwise the DS225+ is cheaper and does the job.

faq.q: Do I need to buy drives separately?
faq.a: For every unit except the Buffalo LinkStation, yes. The others are diskless.
No. RAID protects against a drive failure but not deletion or fire. Keep an offsite copy of key files.

faq.q: Can a 1-bay NAS protect my data?
faq.a: Not alone, since there is no redundancy. Back up to another location.

finalTake: The WD Red Plus 8TB is the right drive to buy for a NAS bay. The Synology DS225+ is the best enclosure for most home offices, with the DS925+ for those who expect growth. The Buffalo LinkStation is the easy starter, and the UGREEN units fill the budget and power ends. Start with CMR and the right bay count.
